title: Where Could UnitedHealth’s Next Growth Come From? - Trefis
content: UnitedHealth Group (UNH) could find its next growth engine in the care it delivers. That perspective carries weight right now. During the company’s October 13 call, management raised its 2026 outlook to adjusted earnings per share of at least $20.50. Yet executives also warned that medical costs remain stubbornly high across health care. So which part of UnitedHealth’s care business still has room to grow? Optum Health Has Room To Add Fully Accountable Patients Optum Health, the care division of the company, is returning to value-based care. Executives noted on the October 13 call that the unit serves 20 million patients, with about 4 million of them in fully accountable relationships. This leaves roughly four in five of those patients outside such arrangements. Management indicated that the business still has room for fully accountable growth. The division continued to deliver strong performance in fiscal Q3 2026. Management said this was driven by the continued return to value-based care principles. The company highlighted high-performing service lines such as home health, hospice and surgery centers. Additionally, the chief financial officer told CNBC that investments in value-based care are taking hold. Questions like this one test every retirement plan. If your advisor recently retired, it is a good moment for a free second opinion from our partner firm. Optum Health generated 22.8% of UnitedHealth’s revenue in fiscal 2025. Optum Rx brought in 34.6%. Combined segment shares exceed 100% because segment revenue can include internal sales between divisions. Even as a major piece of the broader organization, Optum Health shrank last year. Specifically, its revenue fell 3.2% in fiscal 2025. That decline followed 10.5% growth in fiscal 2024. Management has set a margin target for Optum Health of 6% to 8%, calling the effort to get there a multi-year journey. UnitedHealth’s share price rose 16.0% over the year to October 15. title: UNH Stock Outpaces S&P 500 In 2026, Eyes Best Year Since Pandemic — CFO Says Wall Street May Be Missing 2027 Upside - Stocktwits
content: Shares of UnitedHealth (UNH) have outpaced the S&P 500 so far in 2026 and are on pace for their strongest year since 2021. Now, CFO Wayne DeVeydt says Wall Street may be underestimating the company’s earnings opportunity in 2027. UNH stock is up nearly 17% in 2026, outpacing the S&P 500’s 14% gain and the Health Care Select Sector SPDR Fund’s (XLV) 11% rise. The rebound follows a 33% plunge last year. UnitedHealth reported third-quarter (Q3) adjusted earnings of $4.69 per share, topping the $4.14 analyst consensus. Revenue also beat estimates, coming in at $112.69 billion on $111.49 billion, though it was slightly below the $113.2 billion reported a year earlier. Earnings from operations climbed to $6.6 billion from $4.3 billion. The company raised its 2026 adjusted earnings outlook to at least $20.50 per share, from a previous range of $19.50 to $20. But even after its recent rebound, UNH shares are up just 19% since January 2021, a 3% annualized gain over nearly six years. “Current analyst consensus for 2027 may understate the opportunity ahead,” DeVeydt said on the earnings call. He added, “The quality of earnings is strong and durable as we head into 2027.” He called the lower end of UnitedHealth’s long-term adjusted earnings growth target of 13% to 16% a “reasonable starting point.” By Stocktwits’ calculation, 13% growth on the $20.50 floor would imply about $23.17 a share in 2027. Analysts’ quarterly estimates compiled by Fiscal.ai sum to about $22.80. DeVeydt cited share repurchases, value-based care, enterprise-wide progress and gains from artificial intelligence and modernization as potential tailwinds. He also flagged policy reforms, modernization spending, medical-cost trends and pressure on health-benefit funding as headwinds. Quarterly revenue climbed 61% from $70.2 billion in the first quarter of 2021 to $112.7 billion in the third quarter of 2026. Operating profit, however, was nearly unchanged, slipping from $6.7 billion to $6.6 billion. Revenue hovered around $112 billion in the second and third quarters of 2026, while earnings per share swung more sharply. Basic EPS fell to nearly zero in the fourth quarter of 2025, rebounded to $6.90 in the first quarter of 2026, then declined to $6.10 in the second quarter and $4.60 in the third. UnitedHealth reported adjusted EPS of $2.11 for the fourth quarter of 2025. Analysts estimate basic EPS will peak at $8.20 in the first quarter of 2027, then fall to $6.90 in the second quarter, $4.80 in the third and $2.90 in the fourth, according to Fiscal.ai. UnitedHealth’s average 12-month analyst price target is $480.68, implying about 27% upside from current levels. Of 26 analysts, 7 rate the stock ‘Strong Buy,’ 15 ‘Buy’ and 4 ‘Hold’; none rate it ‘Sell’ or ‘Strong Sell,’ according to Koyfin. UnitedHealth’s medical care ratio fell to 88.4% in the third quarter from 89.9% a year earlier, reflecting tighter pricing, benefit changes and cost controls. The result also included $610 million in favorable reserve development. But the ratio rose from 86.7% in the second quarter, and commercial medical trends remained above 11%. When asked whether the trends were worsening, UnitedHealthcare CEO Tim Noel said, “We are not seeing the dynamics that you are talking about.” Medicaid is another pressure point. UnitedHealth expects 2026 to be a trough year for core Medicaid margins, which it now projects to be moderately better than negative 1%. The firm expects margins to return to targeted levels by the end of 2028. At least 69% of UnitedHealthcare’s Medicare Advantage members are in plans rated four stars or higher in the 2027 star ratings, which affect bonus payments in 2028. The company expects that share to reach 75% as it moves through 2027 and into 2028, compared with a 70% industry average. The company plans to focus on high-value Health Maintenance Organization (HMO) plans and special-needs plans for people with chronic conditions or who qualify for both Medicare and Medicaid. UnitedHealthcare is UnitedHealth’s revenue heavyweight, bringing in $86.3 billion in the third quarter. It provides health coverage to employers and individuals and runs the company’s Medicare Advantage and Medicaid plans. Revenue dipped from $87.1 billion a year earlier, but operating earnings climbed to $2.8 billion from $1.8 billion. Optum is the group’s health-services engine. Optum Health delivers care and manages provider networks. Optum Rx handles pharmacy services and prescription benefits. Optum Insight provides tech and data services to healthcare organizations. Together, the businesses generated $66.9 billion in revenue and $3.7 billion in operating earnings. Optum Health’s earnings surged to $735 million from $41 million, while Optum Rx said external clients made up more than half its membership for the first time. Retention remained in the high 90s. Shares of Rocket Lab (RKLB) climbed nearly 1% overnight late Tuesday after an executive said that the company is planning 12 hypersonic test launches this year, spotlighting its role in the U.S. push to develop advanced weapons faster. RKLB stock fell 2% on Tuesday to $64.22, logging its fifth straight session in the red. Rocket Lab’s vice president of global launch services Brian Rogers said that said HASTE enables “low cost, high frequency hypersonic and missile defense testing.” Short for Hypersonic Accelerator Suborbital Test Electron, HASTE is a suborbital test-launch vehicle derived from Rocket Lab’s Electron rocket. It carries experimental payloads for flight testing. Rocket Lab says it can carry payloads of up to 700 kilograms and release them at speeds above 7.5 kilometers per second. The company reported a 100% success rate across HASTE flights in March. “Rather than saying we need to be stuck in an analysis environment and then it’s a very rigorous test campaign that costs a lot of money and involves a lot of people, now you can say we’re planning 12 tests this year,” Rogers told Fox News. “We don’t have to bet the farm on any one of them, which allows us to take more risk and really move the needle in terms of technology development.” The U.S. military is replenishing its missile stockpile, while developing hypersonic weapons, but the systems are costly. Government Accountability Office estimates put the Army’s Dark Eagle missile at more than $40 million each. A Navy estimate for a hypersonic missile planned for Zumwalt destroyers is about $70 million, including development and integration costs. By comparison, a Tomahawk costs about $2.6 million and an Army Precision Strike Missile about $1.6 million. Some startups are targeting lower prices. Castelion says its Blackbeard hypersonic weapon will cost less than $500,000 and is designed for mass production. Rocket Lab has secured a series of contracts for hypersonic testing. In March, it signed a $190 million deal for 20 HASTE flights over four years under the MACH-TB 2.0 program. Anduril followed in May with a $30 million contract for three HASTE test launches. In July, Rocket Lab announced a $266 million Space Force contract for 12 suborbital launches, with options for six more. The missions will primarily launch from a new site in Kodiak, Alaska, with the first expected no earlier than the end of 2026. Rocket Lab said the award will provide high-frequency launch capacity for missile-defense missions. title: CNC, UNH, CVS, HUM Stocks Slip After-Hours — Trump Administration Reportedly Seeks To Scrap Subsidies On Certain Medicare Plans - Stocktwits
content: Shares of health insurance companies, including Centene (CNC), slipped after-hours on Tuesday following a report that the Trump administration plans to end a federal subsidy program that has helped suppress Medicare Part D prescription drug plan premiums. The federal program is currently channeling an estimated $3.6 billion to insurers this year to keep Part D premiums in check. Officials told The Wall Street Journal that the support will expire after 2026 and will not be extended into 2027. The Journal states that about 25 million Americans are enrolled in Part D plans, with the average monthly premium this year running near $36. The Wall Street Journal reports the decision could leave many seniors confronting higher premiums for their stand-alone prescription coverage beginning in 2027. Without the federal support, plan sponsors may pass increased costs to enrollees, potentially accelerating shifts toward Medicare Advantage plans that bundle drug benefits. An administration official quoted by the Journal projected that roughly one-quarter of Part D enrollees will see their premiums hold steady or decline in 2027, about 30% will face hikes under $10 a month, and the remaining 45% will largely see increases in the $11–$20 range. The subsidy primarily benefits insurers offering stand-alone Part D plans (PDPs). Companies with substantial PDP enrollment—UnitedHealth Group (UNH), CVS Health (CVS, via Aetna), Humana (HUM), Centene (CNC, via WellCare), and Molina Healthcare (MOH)—stand to lose this revenue stream. Loss of the $3.6-billion in support could pressure margins if insurers absorb costs or reduce competitiveness through higher premiums, risking enrollment declines. However, beneficiaries might also migrate to Medicare Advantage plans and help offset losses. Centene holds the largest share of stand-alone Medicare Part D (PDP) enrollment via Wellcare — more than eight million members as of early 2026, or about one-third of the entire PDP market, exceeding the exposure of its rivals. CNC shares dived 3% after hours on Tuesday, while shares of UNH, CVS, and HUM fell by about or less than 1%. The initiative, announced on Tuesday by Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy, aims to eliminate red tape for commercial operators as the U.S. prepares for an unprecedented surge in orbital launches and space infrastructure development. Commercial space stocks, including Rocket Lab (RKLB), AST SpaceMobile (ASTS), Intuitive Machines (LUNR), and Planet Labs (PL) dropped between 3% and 7% on Tuesday, while SpaceX (SPCX) added 3%. Under the proposed framework, the FAA would gain the authority to waive requirements established across 13 major federal environmental statutes. These include the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), the Endangered Species Act, the Clean Water Act, and the Clean Air Act. Federal officials emphasized that exemptions would only apply where environmental rules delay innovation, maintaining that core public health, national security, and safety safeguards will remain intact. "America won the first Space Race, and we can do it again -- but only if we get government red tape out of the way," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy stated, noting that the goal is to lower costs and strengthen U.S. competitiveness. Environmental assessments—which currently can take over a year to complete—have long been a target of frustration for commercial launch providers. If you own SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF (NYSEARCA:DIA), UnitedHealth’s share of your fund shrank and swelled along that entire path, driven solely by its share price. State Street Global Advisors describes DIA’s benchmark as a price-weighted index of 30 component common stocks. Price-weighted means one simple rule: the higher a stock’s share price, the bigger its slice of the fund. Company size, earnings, and business quality play no role. As UnitedHealth’s share price fell by half, its influence inside DIA fell with it. As the price climbed back, that influence returned automatically. The fund holds the most of a stock when it is most expensive and the least when it is cheapest. Those shifts come from the weighting rule alone. The relationship above follows directly from the published weighting method. State Street Global Advisors reports UnitedHealth at 4.55% of DIA as of October 14, 2026, making it the fund’s fifth-largest holding. Goldman leads because, under price weighting, the top position is by definition the highest-priced stock. That ranking reflects what one share costs. It says nothing about which business is largest or best run. These weights move every trading day with share prices. The rule that returned UnitedHealth’s role in the rebound also trimmed it on the way down. While the stock slipped from $596.08 to $290.17, DIA’s shrinking position limited the damage compared with a fund holding a fixed percentage. Price weighting cuts exposure to losers and adds exposure to risers. That helps in a sustained decline and hurts in a sharp rebound. Which effect wins depends entirely on the path a stock takes. The method has real strengths, too. The Dow carries an extremely long history, DIA is large and widely held, the methodology is published, and professionals understand it. No single holding wins the fund, so the effect on any one name stays limited. State Street Global Advisors lists DIA’s gross expense ratio at 0.16%, or $16 a year per $10,000 invested. Broad S&P 500 index funds charge as little as 0.03%, about $3 per $10,000. That gap compounds quietly, but it matters less than how the fund decides what you own. A market-cap-weighted fund sizes positions by total company value (share price times shares outstanding), which at least tracks something economic about the business. An equal-weight fund resets every holding to the same slice on a schedule, buying more of whatever has fallen. Price weighting instead follows the number printed on a single share, a number a stock split can cut overnight with no change to the underlying company. If you own DIA because the Dow sounds safe, note that, per State Street Global Advisors, share price alone determines how your money is allocated among its 30 stocks.
